For the provider-specific fields, see Repository Setup. Click Connect. Torque scans the repository and shows a Successfully connected to summary with the number of assets that were discovered and are now managed in the space. Blueprint YAML files under the repository's blueprints folder are added to the space automatically. Note: you can always use this example repository with pre-existing automation assets and blueprints. Click Explore in IaC Assets Page (or go to Automation > Automation Inventory and open the IaC Assets tab). Each discovered asset is listed with its Type, Self-Service and Building Block toggles, Status, IaC Local Path, and Repository Name. Toggle Self-Service for the asset you want to launch. Torque wraps the asset in a blueprint behind the scenes and adds it to the Self-Service catalog. For details, see Blueprint Design.

Terraform runs on a Torque agent. A new space has no agent yet: its Resources → Agents page shows Connect an Agent ("To eventually launch environments, an Agent is required"). Either: Use an existing agent: switch to All Spaces, go to Resources → Agents, open the agent's ⋮ menu, select Manage Spaces, click Add, and select your space. Install your own agent: in the space, go to Resources → Agents, click New Agent, and follow Install an Agent on your Kubernetes Cluster. At the end of the wizard, click Associate to Space. The agent also needs your cloud credentials to provision the environment in your AWS or Azure account. There are two ways to provide them: Credentials store (recommended): Store the credentials once in Automation > Credentials and reference them from a blueprint through a type: credentials input and the grain's authentication block. See Credentials and Credentials Input Type. Environment variables in the blueprint YAML: Author a blueprint YAML file under the blueprints folder of your repository that references the Terraform module as a grain, and expose the credentials as inputs mapped to environment variables, as shown below. The blueprint is added to the space automatically once the repository is synced. For the blueprint structure, see Blueprint Design.
documents.s: Step #3: Choose an agent and add cloud credentials

documents.t: The agent needs your AWS credentials to provision the environment in your AWS account. In your blueprint YAML, expose them as inputs and map them to environment variables so they are provided when a new environment is launched. Add the following inputs under the input section of the blueprint: inputs: AWS_ACCESS_KEY: type: string AWS_SECRET_KEY: type: string Add the following environment variables under the env-var section of the blueprint. For more information about generating AWS credentials, see the AWS documentation env-vars: - AWS_ACCESS_KEY: '{{ .inputs.AWS_ACCESS_KEY }}' - AWS_SECRET_KEY: '{{ .inputs.AWS_SECRET_KEY }}'

The agent needs your Azure credentials to provision the environment in your Azure account. In your blueprint YAML, expose them as inputs and map them to environment variables so they are provided when a new environment is launched. Add the following inputs under the input section of the blueprint: inputs: ARM_CLIENT_ID: type: string ARM_CLIENT_SECRET: type: string ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: type: string ARM_TENANT_ID: type: string Add the following environment variables under the env-var section of the blueprint. For more information about generating Azure credentials, see the Azure documentation env-vars: - ARM_CLIENT_ID: '{{ .inputs.ARM_CLIENT_ID }}' - ARM_CLIENT_SECRET: '{{ .inputs.ARM_CLIENT_SECRET }}' - ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID: '{{ .inputs.ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}' - ARM_TENANT_ID: '{{ .inputs.ARM_TENANT_ID }}'

At this point, you have done the following: Created a new space Connected an asset repository and discovered its assets Chosen an agent and a way to provide cloud credentials 🚀🚀 You are now ready to launch your first environment! 🚀🚀 Make sure the blueprint or IaC asset is published: in Automation > Automation Inventory, the Self-Service toggle of the item must be on (inside a blueprint, the Self Service button reads Hide from Catalog while it is published). See Publishing to the Self-Service Catalog. Go to Self-Service and click Launch on the blueprint card. Specify the environment's name, duration, tags, and inputs. Some of the inputs may be the credentials or agent required to deploy, as described in Step #3. Optionally assign collaborators to the environment. While everyone in the space has "read" permission to its environments, only the environment's owner and collaborators can perform actions that change the environment: extend or end the environment, reconcile or update resource changes, and so on. When launching the environment, the new owner/collaborators receive a notification email if you have Notifications configured in the space. Finally, click Launch. Wait until the environment is active and use it as needed. URLs to the environment's applications are typically provided as outputs - these can be found in the environment's Quick Access links. Check out the Resources tab to get details about your environment's resources. Use this tab to understand what assets each grain spun up, get connection details to specific resources, and more.

This guide walks you through the process of importing an existing environment into Torque, starting from resource curation to final import using the API. Follow these steps to successfully onboard an environment into Torque. Step 1: Curate and codify a Resource​ Start by curating the resource you want to manage in Torque. After curating, you'll obtain the Terraform files and the corresponding tfstate file. Step 2: Edit the Providers File​ Open the providers file within the Terraform files and remove the following sensitive credentials: Access Key Secret Key Token Step 3: Upload Terraform Files to Git​ Upload all the Terraform files, excluding the tfstate file, to your Git repository. For this example, place them under the folder terraform/curate-example. Step 4: Create a Matching Blueprint​ Create a corresponding Torque blueprint for the environment, named curate-example.yaml. Here's an example blueprint: spec_version: 2 inputs: agent: type: 'agent' grains: s3: kind: 'terraform' spec: source: store: 'bps' path: 'terraform/curate-example' agent: name: '{{ .inputs.agent }}' inputs: [] Note: There is no need to specify the Terraform backend in the blueprint. Step 5: Create an S3 Bucket and upload the tfstate File​ Create a new S3 bucket to store the tfstate file, which will act as the Terraform backend for state management. Upload the tfstate file you received during the curation process to the S3 bucket created. Step 6: Use the Import API​ To import the environment using the Torque API, make the following POST request using curl. The API response will include the environment-id. After importing, you will see an import step, followed by an apply step with Torque tags applied to the environment. curl -X POST "https://portal.qtorque.io/api/spaces/{space_name}/environments/import_using_blueprint" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "source": { "blueprint_name": "curate-example", "repository_name": "bps" }, "environment_name": "my-env", "owner_email": "email@quali.com", "grains": [ { "kind": "terraform", "name": "s3", "agent": { "name": "agent-name" }, "backend": { "type": "s3", "bucket": "my-state-bucket", "region": "eu-west-1", "key": "terraform/terraform.tfstate" } } ], "inputs": { "agent": "agent-name" } }'

Destroying Resources: If you are importing a resource that already exists in the cloud, keep in mind that ending the environment in Torque will destroy the resource. To avoid unintended deletion, you can release the environment by running the following API command using curl: curl -X DELETE "https://portal.qtorque.io/api/spaces/{space_name}/environments/{environment_id}/release?force={false/true}" Use the release API to ensure resources are not deleted during the termination process.

To import Terraform states from another account that cannot be accessed directly by the IAM role associated with the agent, follow these steps: 1. Set Up IAM Role in Target Account​ Ensure the IAM role in the target account has a trust relationship that allows the role used in the automation account to assume the target account role. 2. Configure Import Payload​ Add the following to the import payload: curl -X POST "https://portal.qtorque.io/api/spaces/{space_name}/environments/import_using_blueprint" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "grains": [ { "kind": "terraform", "name": "s3", "agent": { "name": "agent-name" }, "backend": { "type": "s3", "bucket": "my-state-bucket", "region": "eu-west-1", "key": "terraform/terraform.tfstate", "role-arn": "<arn-of-target-account-role>" # set up the target role-arn that has access to the bucket and key configured above } } ] }' Important Notes​ Terraform version 1.5.7 is recommended. You can set it in the blueprint or in the import request You might need to use another role in the blueprint as well, using the provider-overrides feature info Make sure to provide the Torque authentication token. This can be a short or long-token The source section points to the blueprint generated and the repository name onboarded to Torque. The backend section added in under the grain should point to the state file exported and uploaded to the backend of choice. By following these steps, you'll be able to successfully import and manage an environment in Torque while ensuring security and state management.
documents.s: Importing Terraform State from Another AWS Account

documents.t: An agent is the component that communicates with your Torque tenant and creates the required environment resources. It executes, manages, and monitors the workloads that Torque deploys on your behalf. This quick-start guide walks you through the fastest path to get Torque up and running: connecting a single agent. Unlike blueprint-driven onboarding, an agent does not require a space or a repository — you can install it on its own and associate it with spaces and repositories later. In this guide we will cover: Where an agent can be installed (cloud or on-premises) Generating the deployment for your agent Installing the agent and verifying that it is connected (Optional) Associating the agent with a space and launching blueprints from a repository What is an agent? The agent is a lightweight orchestration component deployed in your own environment. Once connected, it appears in Resources → Agents, where you can monitor its health (Connected / Disconnected), type, version, and IP. Torque supports several agent types, including virtual machine images (OVA), managed Kubernetes (for example EKS), Docker, and self-managed Kubernetes.

Navigate to Resources → Agents. Review the list of existing agents. The page shows an at-a-glance Health and Type breakdown, plus a table with each agent's Name, Status, Type, Version, and IP. Click New Agent in the top-right corner to open the Connect an Agent wizard.

In the Setup step, select where you would like to install your agent: Option Description Cloud Install into a public or GPU cloud. After choosing this option, select Public Cloud or GPU Cloud. On-Premises Install as a virtual machine (VM) in your own datacenter. After choosing this option, select the VM type and then the hypervisor: VMWare, Redhat KVM, or Nutanix. Make your selection and click Next. note The remaining steps depend on your choice. Installing on VMware adds an optional Add Credentials step for your vCenter (covered below). Cloud installations skip that step and go straight to the installation instructions. This guide follows the On-Premises → VM → VMWare path as an example.

In the Generate Agent step, fill in the details Torque needs to build the deployment for your agent. Field Required Description Example Agent Name Yes A unique, human-readable name for the agent. mgmt-vcenter-97 VM Hostname Yes The hostname to assign to the deployed virtual machine. mgmt-vcenter-97 IP Address Yes The static IP address the agent will use. 192.168.1.10 Gateway Yes The default gateway IP address for the VM's network. 192.168.1.1 Subnet Mask Bits (CIDR Notation) Yes The subnet mask expressed as CIDR bits. 24 NTP Servers Yes One or more NTP servers (comma-separated) used to keep the VM's clock in sync. pool.ntp.org,pool2.ntp.org DNS Server No The DNS server IP address the VM should use for name resolution. 192.168.1.53 Location No The geographic location of the agent, selected from the city search. Austin, United States Proxy No Toggle on to route the agent's outbound traffic through an HTTP/HTTPS proxy, then provide the proxy details. — When all required fields are complete, click Next. tip Hover over the ⓘ icon next to any field for inline guidance. Use a static IP that is reserved for the agent so its address does not change after deployment.

For the VMware path, the wizard adds an Add vCenter Credentials (Optional) step (shown as Add Credentials in the step list). It lets you store the vCenter credentials that Torque will later use when this vCenter is added as a target Provider. This step is optional: you can skip it now and add the target credentials later from Resources → Inventory. Adding them now can save time if the agent is deployed in a network with access to your internal vCenter, because you complete the setup in one flow instead of returning later to create the same credentials. note Credential connectivity can be tested only after the agent is deployed and connected to Torque. Choose an account scoped to the target datacenter or cluster rather than a full administrator account where possible. Enter the credentials (or leave the step empty) and click Next.
documents.s: Step #4: Add vCenter credentials (VMware only, optional)

documents.t: The final Installation Instructions step prepares the agent appliance for your chosen target: SSH private key - Torque generates an SSH key for authenticating to the appliance. Copy and save it now; it is not accessible after you close the wizard. Download Agent File - Torque builds the agent OVA file (this takes approximately two minutes). Click Download to save it. Finish stays disabled until the OVA file has been downloaded. Follow the on-screen Instructions to deploy the appliance: Go to your ESX server. Click Create or Register a VM and follow the steps. Select the downloaded .ova file and make sure the network adapter that allows external connectivity is selected before you click Finish. For cloud targets, this step instead shows a command (for example a kubectl-based command for Kubernetes) that you run against your cluster, followed by a Connections Status panel. info It may take up to a couple of minutes for a freshly deployed agent to start up and register. Wait for the Connected indication before continuing.

Return to Resources → Agents. Your new server should appear in the list with a green Connected status. If it still shows Disconnected after a few minutes, confirm that the VM is powered on and that it has outbound network access (and correct proxy settings, if configured) to reach your Torque tenant. 🎉 That's it — your agent is connected and ready to deploy blueprints from the Self-Service Catalog.
A connected agent is fully functional on its own, but to start deploying from blueprints you'll typically pair it with a space and a repository.

Spaces are logically separate areas that group agents, repositories, and permitted users. To let a space deploy through your new agent: From the agent's actions menu (or the post-connection dialog), choose Associate to space. Select the target space. Set the default namespace and service account that Torque will use to deploy workloads through this server. These defaults can be changed later in Resources → Agents.
documents.s: Associate the agent with a space

documents.t: Once an agent is associated with a space, you can connect a repository to that space, discover its automation assets, and generate blueprints from them. Publishing a blueprint to the space catalog lets end-users launch environments — Torque will execute those environments through the associated agent. For the full workflow, see the guides on creating a space, connecting a repository, and launching an environment.
Torque has two navigation areas: the top bar, with the space selector and account-wide tools, and the sidebar, with the pages of the selected space or of the whole account.

Element Description Space selector Shows the current space, or All Spaces when you work on account-level pages. Click it to switch to another space or to create one. The top bar takes on the color of the selected space. See Working with Spaces. Copilot Opens Torque Copilot. See Using Torque Copilot. AI Integrations Opens the AI Integrations panel for connecting external AI tools to Torque. See AI Integrations. Support Opens the Support drawer. See Support. User menu Shows your email and has Log out. Use Account to switch between the Torque accounts you belong to, API Keys to manage your API keys, and Time Zone to set the time zone in which Torque shows dates and times. See API Tokens. Whether you see Copilot, AI Integrations, and the Contact Us section of the Support drawer depends on the permissions of your role. If a team member can't see them, review their role in Admin > User Management. See Roles and Permissions.

The sidebar groups the pages by what you do with them. Click a group to expand or collapse it. The Collapse button at the top of the sidebar reduces it to icons; click Expand to restore it. The items you see depend on whether a space or All Spaces is selected, and on your role. Pages that work only inside a space are disabled in the All Spaces view, with a tooltip that asks you to select a space. Group Inside a space In All Spaces Self-Service The catalog of blueprints and workflows published in the space. The items published in all spaces. Environments The Operation Hub: the environments and workflow executions of the space. The environments and executions of all spaces, with a Space column. Resources Inventory and Agents. Same. Automation Automation Inventory, Credentials, and Repositories. Automation Inventory is disabled. Governance Policies, Approval Requests, Notifications, Users, and Tags. Policies, Policy Repositories, Approval Channels, Approval Requests, Notifications (disabled), and Tags. Reports Opens the account-level Reports page and switches the selector to All Spaces. The Activity, Cost, Realized Savings, Opportunity Savings, and Inventory Utilization tabs. Admin At the bottom of the sidebar: Spaces, User Management, Configurations, Cost Configurations, Account and Billing, and API Keys. Opening an Admin page switches the selector to All Spaces. Same. tip Page URLs follow the selection: the pages of a space start with /<space-name>/, and account-level pages start with /admin/. You can bookmark either.

The Support icon in the top bar opens the Support drawer: Ask Copilot: Start a New Chat with Copilot opens a new Copilot chat. See Using Torque Copilot. Documentation: Explore Documentation opens this documentation site. Contact Us: Ask a question, Ready to share your feedback?, and Report a bug or an issue open the Contact Us form on its Question, Feedback, or Bug tab. Each tab asks for a Subject, a description, and a Severity level, and lets you attach images. Click Submit to send the form, or Cancel to close it. REST API: Explore REST API opens the REST API reference. See REST API.

If you used the previous Torque interface, this table shows where its sidebar pages are now. Previous interface Current interface Account Center in the space list All Spaces in the space selector Self-Service Self-Service Operate > Operation Hub Environments (the page is still titled Operation Hub) Operate > Reports Reports Operate > Approval Requests Governance > Approval Requests Design > Automation Inventory Automation > Automation Inventory Design > Input Sources, Parameters Automation > Credentials, on the Input Sources and Parameters tabs Settings > Repositories Automation > Repositories Settings > Credentials Automation > Credentials Settings > Agents Resources > Agents Settings > Cost Configurations (Account Center) Admin > Cost Configurations Curate > Resources Inventory (Account Center) Resources > Inventory Governance > Tags, Policies, Users Governance > Tags, Policies, Users Governance > Notification Channels Governance > Notifications Governance > Policy Repositories, Approval Channels (Account Center) Governance > Policy Repositories, Approval Channels Governance > User Management (Account Center) Admin > User Management Admin > Spaces, Configurations, Account & Billing (Account Center) Admin > Spaces, Configurations, Account and Billing
Use + Add Provider (top right of the inventory) to launch the two-step Add Provider wizard.

Select the provider type and supply core identity and sharing settings. Choose a provider type. Select from Azure, AWS, vCenter, Kubernetes, OpenShift, RKE2, GCP, or Custom. Tiles marked Coming soon are not available yet. The selected type determines which capabilities become available in Step 2. The Samples tile adds a sample provider so that you can explore the inventory without connecting your own account; an account can have only one sample provider. Provider Alias Name. Enter a unique, human-readable name. It may contain letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores. This alias appears in the inventory list and wherever the provider is referenced as a target. Connected Space(s). Toggle Share with all spaces, or select specific spaces. Any blueprint in a connected space can use this provider's content. Labels (optional). Add or create key:value labels to organize and later filter providers. Advanced Permission Options. Choose how credentials are scoped: Single Credentials Set — use the same credential set for both Discovery and Deploy capabilities. Multiple Credentials Set — use different credential sets for Discovery and Deploy, for least-privilege separation. Click Next. The button stays disabled until the required fields are filled.

Configure the capabilities the chosen provider type supports. With Multiple Credentials Set, this step is split into a Deploy Capability step and a Discovery Capability step. Integration and Permissions — select the cloud credentials the capability uses. The credentials must have the permissions the capability needs: read access for Discovery, and permission to create resources for Deploy. Agent — select the agent that runs discovery scans and deployments for this provider. See What is an Agent? Kubernetes, OpenShift, and RKE2 providers also ask for a Service Account Name and a Namespace. Under Advanced - Runner Management, you can set the Default Runners Namespace and Default Runners Service Account. Runners are the containers Torque creates in your cluster to run provisioning jobs; a dedicated namespace keeps automation isolated from your workloads, and the service account determines the permissions the runners have in the cluster. Click Skip for now to skip a capability step; on the last step, Skip and Done finishes the wizard without it. You can add a skipped capability later from the provider's details panel. Click Cancel to leave the wizard without saving.

The new provider appears in the provider list with its capability icons. If a capability shows red, hover over its icon to see the error, and use Edit Credentials or Discovery Details to fix it. See Reading capability status at a glance. To let end users pick the provider when they launch an environment, give it a Deploy capability and add a target input to the blueprint. See Provider Capabilities.

Available capabilities differ by provider type. The matrix below shows typical support; the wizard reflects the exact options for each selection. Provider Type Discovery Deploy Typical Resources AWS Yes Yes Cloud objects (compute, storage, networking) Azure Yes Yes Cloud objects (compute, storage, networking) GCP Yes Yes Cloud objects (compute, storage, networking) vCenter Yes Yes Virtual machines, datastores, networks Kubernetes, OpenShift, RKE2 Yes Yes Clusters, namespaces, workloads Custom Varies Varies Defined by the custom integration
This page provides a customer-facing overview of what is included in the Torque Agent OVA.
The OVA is a preconfigured management appliance that includes the core building blocks required to run Torque environments on customer infrastructure.
Enterprise Linux base image (AlmaLinux 9.7 or Rocky Linux 9.x, depending on the selected template).
Container runtime and compose tooling used by Torque components during environment operations.
Built-in private container registry capability for storing and serving container images required for automated environments.
DNS capability used for environment-level name resolution scenarios. HTTP file serving capability used for image/file distribution workflows (for example, ISO hosting).
Encrypted local secrets vault mechanism for storing operational credentials used by the agent flows.
VMware guest tooling required for OVF/guestinfo-based configuration at environment time.
Built-in first-boot configuration flow. Built-in update mechanism for post-environment improvements and maintenance tasks.

The table below lists the primary system services that are part of the Torque Agent footprint. Service name (systemd) Included in base image Enabled at boot Typical start phase Customer-facing role sshd Yes Yes Base OS runtime Administrative access vmtoolsd Yes Yes Image build/install VMware guest integration torque_service Yes Yes First boot runtime Torque bootstrap and lifecycle control docker Yes Yes First boot configure Container runtime for platform capabilities devpi Yes Yes First boot configure Internal package/cache capability used by platform flows httpd Yes Yes First boot configure HTTP file distribution capability named Yes Yes First boot configure DNS capability harbor.service Created during configure Yes (after creation) First boot configure Container registry capability zt-cleaner.service Added by update flow Yes (after installation) Post-environment update Storage maintenance and cleanup note Service composition can vary slightly by release and update level. Some services are platform-internal and are not intended for direct day-to-day customer operation.

The image is built so that component network exposure is controlled during configuration, after required credentials/settings are applied. Security hardening steps are applied as part of the provisioning/bootstrap process.

Depending on the enabled capabilities and your environment model, typical ports include: 22/tcp (SSH) 80/tcp (HTTP file serving) 53/tcp and 53/udp (DNS) 5000/tcp and 5001/tcp (container registry endpoints)
Final package composition can vary slightly by image build path and version.

Torque Resources Inventory gives you a single, governed view of every infrastructure and cloud endpoint your organization connects to. Each entry in the inventory is a provider — a connection to a cloud account, virtualization platform, Kubernetes cluster, or infrastructure controller — that doubles as a target for discovery and deployment operations. In practice, a provider pairs an agent with the credentials for its Discovery and Deploy capabilities, and blueprint YAML references the provider through the target input type. Providers are typed on creation (for example AWS, Azure, vCenter, Kubernetes, OpenShift, RKE2, GCP, or Custom). A provider's type determines which capabilities it can offer. The two core capabilities are: Discovery — the provider can be scanned to enumerate the resources it manages (for example virtual machines, Kubernetes workloads, or cloud objects), which are then browsable inside the inventory. Deploy — the provider can be used as a target for deploying blueprints and launching environments. The inventory surface aggregates health and distribution metrics across all providers so operators can quickly assess coverage, spot unhealthy connections, and understand which capabilities are active across the estate. The Resources → Inventory page has two tabs: Tab Content Providers Health and capability metrics, the provider list, Recent Collections, and Add Provider. See Providers Inventory. Custom Resources Resource types and instances that you define and that blueprints can reserve. See Custom Resources.

Term Description Provider A connection to an external system (cloud, virtualization, Kubernetes, infrastructure controller). Each provider is also a deployment target. Provider Type The category selected at creation (AWS, Azure, vCenter, Kubernetes, OpenShift, RKE2, GCP, Custom). Determines available capabilities. Capability A function a provider exposes — primarily Discovery and Deploy. Availability depends on provider type and configuration. Resource An individual item discovered under a provider (e.g., a VM, a Kubernetes workload, or a cloud object). Spaces The space(s) a provider is shared with; controls which blueprints can use the provider's content. Capability Health A rolled-up indicator of how many providers have a working Discovery or Deploy capability. Credential set The cloud credentials a capability uses. A provider can use one set for both capabilities or a separate set for each. See Credential sets. Collection A set of discovered resources that you codify into Terraform or curate into a live environment. See Codifying and Curating Resources. Custom resource An instance of a resource type that you define, which blueprints can reserve at launch. See Custom Resources.

The inventory is controlled per account in Admin > Configurations > Resources Inventory, which has two toggles: Cloud Resources enables provider discovery, so that you can codify unmanaged resources and curate selected resources into managed Torque environments. Custom Resources enables the Custom Resources tab, with resource types and instances that blueprints can reserve. If both are turned off, the Inventory page asks you to enable the inventory from the Configurations page. See Resources Inventory.

An AWS Account. Enable AWS Resource Explorer Steps to Enable AWS Resource Explorer Service: Navigate to the AWS Management Console Click the Turn on Resource Explorer button on the right of the screen, go to step 3 if already enabled Follow the steps and select an Aggregator index Region, take note of the region Go to the Views tab under Explore Resources on the left side Create a new view or use the existing all-resources view Get the ARN of the view, it should look like the ARN below for the "all-resources" view arn:aws:resource-explorer-2:"your-region":"your-account":view/all-resources/"some-guid" info The Resource Explorer indexing process, once turned on, can take up to 72 hours to complete. If a resource does not show up in Resource Explorer, it will not show up in the Torque inventory. Create an IAM User Create an IAM User under the IAM Service Give a Permission Policy to that user. Minimum policy is AWSResourceExplorerReadOnlyAccess. Ideal policy is ReadOnlyAccess explained under Minimal Permissions Required Create Access Keys under Security credentials and take note of the Access and Secret Keys values info Currently the only authentication method supported is IAM Users with an Access and Secret Keys, additional authentications are coming in the near future

Torque Resources Inventory requires read-only access to inventory and manage cloud resources. The following permissions are required: AWSResourceExplorerReadOnlyAccess assigned to the IAM User. This only gives you the ability to see resources in the inventory. For the ability to convert resources in Terraform or manage environments, ReadOnlyAccess is recommended so all resource types can be used.

AWS accounts are connected as Providers with the Discovery capability: Go to Resources → Inventory, open the Providers tab, and click Add Provider. In Provider Details, select the AWS tile, enter a Provider Alias Name, choose the Connected Space(s), optionally add Labels, and click Next. In All Capabilities, enable Discovery and, under Integration and Permissions, provide the read-only credentials you prepared: the Account Number, Access Key, Secret Key, and the View Arn of your Resource Explorer view. Select the agent that will run the discovery. Save the provider. Once the Discovery capability shows as healthy, Torque begins scanning and discovering your cloud resources. For the wizard details, see Adding a Provider.

Torque Cloud Resources gives you visibility and governance over the resources that already exist in your cloud accounts. You connect a cloud account as a Provider with the Discovery capability, and Torque scans the account with read-only permissions, inventories every resource it finds, and lets you filter the inventory by type, location, or Infrastructure as Code (IaC) status. Torque classifies discovered resources by their IaC status: Unmanaged: Resources that were created manually and are not governed by IaC. Codified: Resources that are managed by your existing IaC. Managed: Resources that are managed by Torque environments. From the inventory you can add resources to a Collection and either Codify them into Terraform configuration and state files, or Curate them straight into a live Torque environment.

Cloud Resource Discovery: Automatically discovers and inventories the resources in each connected cloud account, providing a holistic view of your cloud estate. Resource Filtering: Filter resources by keyword, type, location, IaC status, tags, and attributes. IaC Integration: Generate Terraform files and state for unmanaged resources, simplifying the transition of manually provisioned resources into IaC. Codify and Curate: Select resources into a Collection, then download them as Terraform artifacts or curate them into a managed environment.

Cloud accounts are added as Providers in Resources → Inventory. Click Add Provider, choose the cloud tile, and enable the Discovery capability with read-only credentials. For the account-side prerequisites, see: AWS Azure For the wizard itself, see Adding a Provider and Provider Capabilities.

Once a provider's Discovery capability is healthy, Torque scans the account and inventories its resources. To browse them: Go to Resources → Inventory and open the Providers tab. Click the provider name, or open its ⋮ menu and select View Resources. The resource list shows each resource's Resource Name, Type, IaC Status, Location, and Last Modified date. Use Search by keyword and Filters to narrow the list by type, location, IaC status, tags, or attributes.

Clicking a resource opens its details drawer: Resource Status: The Resource Type, IaC Status, Location, Resource ID (for example, the AWS ARN), and Resource API Identifier. Cloud Account: The Provider, the Cloud Account the resource was discovered from, and when it was Last Synced. Add to Collection: Adds the resource to the current Collection (see below).
Resources are codified or curated through a Collection, a working set of resources from a single provider.

In the provider's resource list, tick the checkbox of each resource you want to include, or click Add to Collection in a resource's details drawer. Use the header checkbox to add every resource on the page. Click Collection at the top right to open the Current Collection panel and review the selected resources. You can remove individual resources or Clear the whole collection. note A Collection can only contain resources from the same provider. Resources with the IaC status Managed cannot be curated.

In the Current Collection panel, click Codify. Review the Codify Summary. Torque creates a ZIP folder containing a Terraform file with state for the selected resources. Confirm. Codification may take up to a minute. You can close the dialog and follow the progress in the Recent Collections panel. When the codification completes, download the ZIP from Recent Collections (the Codifications list).

Curating imports the resources into a managed Torque environment in one flow: In the Current Collection panel, click Curate as Environment. Fill in the Environment Details: the Environment Name, the Space Name to launch in, the Agent that will run the Terraform, and the Repository and Branch where the generated Terraform files are stored. Click Approve & Curate. Torque generates the Terraform files and state, uploads them to the repository, discovers and imports the new asset, generates a blueprint, and launches the environment. Follow the progress in the Recent Collections panel (the Curations list), then click Go to Environment.

The Terraform configuration and state files generated by Torque can be used to manage your cloud resources through Infrastructure as Code. Possible actions include: Integration with Existing IaC Projects: Incorporate the generated Terraform files into existing IaC projects to maintain consistency in infrastructure management. Manage Resources via Terraform: Utilize the generated files to manage manually provisioned resources, simplifying their incorporation into existing IaC frameworks. Resource Deployment and Modification: With Terraform, apply, modify, or destroy cloud resources, granting precise control over curated infrastructure. Version Control: Store the Terraform files in a version control system such as Git, enabling collaborative management, change tracking, and versioning of infrastructure. Import into Torque: Follow Import Cloud Resources to turn codified resources into a managed environment through the API.

To maximize the benefits of Torque Resources Inventory, consider the following best practices: Tag Resources Consistently: Ensure that all cloud resources are tagged appropriately for easier filtering and curation. Keep Discovery Healthy: Watch the Capabilities Health card and the Discovery icon of each provider so the inventory stays up to date. CI/CD Integration: Integrate downloaded Terraform files into CI/CD pipelines to automate infrastructure deployment and management processes. Periodic IaC Status Review: Regularly review the IaC status of resources to identify unmanaged entities and bring them under proper governance.

documents.t: Cloud resources can be discovered from AWS, Azure, and GCP providers. The Providers inventory also discovers resources from vCenter and Kubernetes providers; see Provider Capabilities.
Discovery requires read-only permissions to the cloud account, for example the Reader role on an Azure subscription or a read-only IAM policy on AWS. See the AWS and Azure setup pages for details.
documents.s: What Permissions Are Required for Torque Resources Inventory?

documents.t: Yes, you can modify the generated Terraform files to suit your specific requirements before utilizing them in your IaC workflows.
documents.s: Can I Edit the Generated Terraform Files?

documents.t: If the provider's Discovery capability shows as unhealthy, verify the following: The provided credentials have read-only permissions. The account identifiers (subscription ID, account number, view ARN) are accurate. There are no network or firewall settings preventing the agent from accessing the cloud account.
